paras: The clubbing of Mr. Hill by Officer Palmer was a police beating in Tarrytown in about mid-January 1903, reported in a dispatch dated January 26 as having occurred "about a week ago." The correspondent called the clubbing "unnecessary" and reported that the Black residents of "both villages" secured a lawyer for Hill, presenting the case as part of a wider demand for their rights.

The dispatch that reported Hill's clubbing opened with a different matter: the authorities, it said, had offered a $100 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the murderer or murderers of Samuel Wisner. The correspondent credited the reward to a "stirring appeal" by Rev. C. W. Randall and presented it as a sign that the colored people of the place had to be recognized.

According to the correspondent, Officer Palmer clubbed Hill about a week before January 26, 1903. The dispatch gives neither man's first name, Palmer's department, nor the circumstances of the encounter, and it does not say whether Hill was arrested or charged.

The clubbing "agitated" the colored citizens of both villages, who secured counsel for Hill and were "determined to have his case vindicated." No report of a hearing, a complaint against Palmer, or any outcome of the case was found in the coverage.

The episode appears only in the American Citizen, as a short item in a Tarrytown news letter printed on page one under the headline "Reward in Murder Case" on January 30, 1903; no white-press report of the clubbing was found. The same paper printed the dispatch again, unchanged, on February 6. Writing in the first person plural, the correspondent framed both the reward and the legal defense of Hill as gains won by the community, closing: "Our rights come high, but we must have them."
